Posted November 14, 2007 

Analysis by Richard Cowan  

MarijuanaNews.com: I am pleased to post an Op-ed by my old friend Mike Cutler that was published last August in the Providence Journal. It has taken on an added relevance now that John Edwards has been endorsed by Ben Cohen, co-founder of Ben and Jerrys ice cream.  

 

This ex-hippy turned hip capitalist is an icon of American business/culture. His endorsement was not just his personal action. Cohen founded and funds a group calledCaucus4Priorities.  

 

According to the AP, the group is dedicated to cutting wasteful Pentagon spending and claims it has 10,000 Iowa members who promise to vote for Edwards in the Jan. 3 caucuses. 

 

I think that this focus on wasteful Pentagon spending is admirable, but  as my friend explains below  not nearly enough.  

 

Edwards is a whole hearted drug warrior who explicitly opposed even the decriminalization of cannabis  which seems to be supported by a majority of Americans  because it would send the wrong message to children. Thus he supports the arrest of 800,000 Americans per year based on the most brainless of the prohibitionist clichés.  

See 

The Clichés of Prohibitionism: "Sending the Wrong Message." 

This line is particularly ironic for the former Senator from North Nicotinia (Carolina), whose state is the heart of the tobacco industry. Somehow, I dont recall him urging the arrest of tobacco growers, much less smokers, regardless of the message.   

 

However, nothing can approach the irony of a fortune built on the munchies and a crunchy image being used to support a candidate who disapproves of the image implicit in his benefactors marketing. 

 

Readers may recall that I have been very critical of the anti-war lefts refusal to confront the drug war, and Cohens endorsement of Edwards is just one more very sad example. 

See 

Sicko and The Return of MarijuanaNews.com. The Failure of the Left to Address the Drug War. By Richard Cowan.  

And 

Will Plan Mexico And Its Surge in the Drug War Put Prohibition On the Public Agenda? Analysis by Richard Cowan
 and
 The Drug War Is Politics By Other Means: Blackwater Gets Billions to Fight Narco-Terorism. Buying Constituencies for the Drug War. Analysis by Richard Cowan 

Of course, to be fair to Edwards, he does get an A- fromGranite Staters for Medical Marijuana. He has repeatedly said that he would stop the raids in medical marijuana states. Realistically, that is all that a President can do without Congress, other than rescheduling cannabis. 

 

However, Edwards is also quoted by the Granite Staters as saying,
I really think that we need to put the FDA in charge of this instead of having -- right now it's just a political football. I think if we give the FDA the responsibility and have them determine how to treat this -- somebody like you who needs medical marijuana to ease your pain and there's not other medications that can accomplish it, then the FDA can say that. But what we have right now is a situation where it's a huge political football, it's used for political rhetoric, and the result is a lot of people are being punished as a result. And so that's what I would do, I would put it under the responsibility of the FDA and I would stop these raids. That's what I would do." 

 

It is hard to believe that someone who has been a Senator and a lawyer could think that the FDA would be the solution to anything, and this statement would also seem to imply that patients would have to prove there's not other medications that can accomplish it No, thanks. There is no reason that patients should have to suffer for the right to use something that works.  

See 

In Their Own Words: FDA Press Release On New Anti-Nausea Drug For Chemotherapy Patients Prove Prohibitionists Are Lying About Need For Medical Cannabis. Officially Recommended Doses Of FDA Approved Medicines Often Too High;
Mike Cutlers message is addressed to Edwards, but the rest of the candidates  and indeed the antiwar left  would do well to consider its message. It is the right message for candidates. And it would go well with some Cherry Garcia ice cream.) 

By Michael D. Cutler, Esq., Brookline, MA 

michaeldcutler@aim.com  

John Edwards chances of passing Hillary Clinton and Barak Obama for the presidential nomination are slim and none. Edwards needs a more compelling plan to lift America and portray leadership, or else his campaign is doomed. Clinton and Obama will not be out-spent, out-organized or out-messaged, unless Edwards seizes voter interest on an issue with the impact of the Iraq War. Re-declaring war on poverty will not pass his competitors, and declaring peace in Iraq is not a distinction. 

  

Edwards chance for leadership requires his challenge to an older and more destructive war ignored by the front-runners, the War on Drugs (killing many times more Americans than terrorism and the Iraq War combined). Drug reform has presidential and popular precedence, and its no gamble since Edwards is certain to lose currently. Governor Al Smith led New York out of the violence and health crisis of Alcohol Prohibition, and overcame anti-Catholic prejudice to seize the nomination in 1928. FDR parlayed prohibition reform into victory. Reform adoption in several states (diversion of nonviolent offenders to treatment instead of detention, approval of clean needles, methadone maintenance and medical marijuana) demonstrates mainstream support.  

 

Drug War reform can command attention while distinguishing Edwards from Clinton and Obama. Both war policies are remarkably similar examples that "the Emperor wears no clothes," the recognition of which can change the order of the front-runners.  

 

Like the Iraq War, the Drug War exemplifies the principle "garbage-in, garbage-out."  

See
Bush Should Have John  Comical Ali  Walters Explain The Iraq War, Then The Media Would Never Ask Any Embarrassing Questions. Doctrine Of Drug Czar Infallibility? Blame Canada, Again.  

Because both policies fundamental predicates are impractical aspirations divorced from reality, the results are counter-productive. Zero-tolerance is nonsense in a world of caffeine and anti-depressants. Supply interdiction of globally available plants defies common sense. Punishment never has restrained addiction. Prohibition still fails to promote abstinence and always is corrupted by capitalism. The Drug Wars foundation, conflicting with basic human instincts, dooms it to worsening abuse just as the Iraq Wars reliance on force instead of negotiation encourages terrorism. Built on impossible expectations, both wars collateral damage beggars any temporary illusion of progress. 

 

Edwards should promote Drug War reform and link its chaos to the Iraq fiasco, generating a winning conversation for two reasons. First, the Drug Wars failure is obvious to most Americans, being everyone with a family member at risk of drug abuse, or who is experiencing or has survived abuse. Drug War advocates claim, that reform-reduced punishment sends the "wrong message" to children or addicts, has no more credibility than the troop surge to facilitate tribal reconciliation. More or better punishment obviously is not the answer to either problem.  

 

Second, Drug War reform like the Iraq War requires an admission that the candidates former war support was wrong. Edwards courage to admit both wars mistakes can project a strength contrasting with Clintons balky Iraq War evolution. Edwards can effectively cross-examine Clinton on her support for incarceration and preemptive force in Iraq, given his skill and her record. Edwards' only risk is Obamas adoption of this issue. Obama could use the Drug Wars naked racism to powerful advantage. He is unlikely to appreciate this opportunity, however, given Obamas lack of experience in campaigns and government. Taking no position (or worse, opposing reform) to protect his poll standing could jeopardize Obamas core support. 

 

Attacking the Drug War on the same terms as the Iraq War is an underdogs dream. The media loves this issue, and Edwards' adoption of this historical "third rail" issue is an epic storyline. The front-runners embrace of the "conventional wisdom" behind chronically bipartisan Drug War-making would indefensibly endorse a status quo that tolerates this worsening health and safety problem. 

 

By demonstrating a leaders courage, Edwards can grow his support and wilt his competitors. Or, he can hammer societys chronic tolerance for poverty, until Edwards stands on the convention podium behind the partys nominee.
